sections.html:
Enfield sits on the Massachusetts line in Hartford County, with the Connecticut River along its western edge. It belongs to the Capitol Planning Region, and its area is 34.2 square miles, of which 0.93 is water. Longmeadow and East Longmeadow, Massachusetts, lie to the north, Somers to the east, East Windsor and Ellington to the south, and Suffield and Windsor Locks across the river.

The 2020 census counted 42,141 residents, and the elevation is about 138 feet. With that much land, housing runs from compact village lots to rural parcels, and the buyer pool changes from section to section. It was settled in 1679 and joined Connecticut in 1749, after a surveyor's error was found to have placed it in the wrong colony.

Five traditional sections make up the town: Enfield Village, Thompsonville, Hazardville, Scitico and Sherwood Village. Named neighborhoods inside and around them are what sellers use to describe a house.

  • Thompsonville: the urban center on the river, with Victorian houses along Pearl Street and boat launches onto the Connecticut River.
  • Hazardville: a village center on Hazard Avenue, Powder Hollow Park and the Enfield Public Library.
  • Enfield Historic District: along Enfield Street (U.S. Route 5), with homes from the mid-eighteenth century on and a Greek Revival church.
  • Scitico and Green Manor: a suburb on the east side, with winding roads, cul-de-sacs and sidewalks, about 4.5 miles from I-91.
  • Shaker Pines: lakeside houses on a lake the Shakers built to power a mill.
  • Presidential Section: streets named for U.S. presidents, with mid-sized to large houses.

Crescent Lake, North Thompsonville, The Laurels and Southwood Acres are other names buyers know.

Part of the housing here is truly old, and buyers of historic or early houses look closely at age. The Enfield Town Meetinghouse, built in 1773, and the Enfield Historic District along Route 5 are on the National Register of Historic Places. So are the Bigelow-Sanford Carpet Company buildings in Thompsonville, now apartments called Bigelow Commons.

Orrin Thompson built carpet mills in Thompsonville along with housing for the workers, and much of that housing still stands. Before repairs on a house in or beside the historic district, check with the town's land use staff for limits on exterior work. Whatever its age, a buyer's inspector will study the roof, wiring, heating system and foundation, and a problem in any of them can slow a conventional sale.

For the current bill dates, the mill rate and the exact payoff on your parcel, call the Enfield Tax Collector and the Assessor or visit enfield-ct.gov.

The Grand List is the yearly record of taxable property, and Connecticut towns revalue every five years. Because a new assessment moves the tax a buyer will carry, find out from Enfield's assessor when the next one lands.

Taxes owed on your property are settled from your sale proceeds at closing, so request a written payoff early.

Connecticut has the grantor, or an attorney or agent acting for the grantor, file a conveyance tax return as the deed is recorded. A price of $2,000 or more is taxed unless an exemption fits, and the Department of Revenue Services shows Enfield as town code 049.

The filing may be electronic through the state's myCTREC system or on paper with the town clerk, depending on the town, and the Enfield Town Clerk will tell you which. Exemptions that matter to sellers:

  • A conveyance between spouses.
  • Giving up a principal residence by deed in lieu of foreclosure.
  • A principal residence that sells for less than its mortgages and priority tax or sewer liens.
  • A pyrrhotite-damaged concrete foundation on a principal residence, backed by a professional engineer's written evaluation.

An exemption needs its code on the return and may need an attachment. Your closing attorney can confirm which apply.

sections.h2: Documents to gather before asking for offers
sections.html:
Sellers who come prepared close faster. Most of what a title company asks for fits on a short list.

  • The deed, or the estate papers showing who may sign.
  • A written tax payoff from the Enfield Tax Collector.
  • Payoff statements for any mortgage or lien.
  • Any lease, if tenants live in the house.
  • Names of the electric, water and heating suppliers for final readings.

If a piece is missing, tell us anyway. Gaps in the paperwork can often be worked around, and it is easier to sort them out at the start than in the last week.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works in Enfield
sections.html:
Enfield owners often hold an older house that needs work, an inherited property, a rental or a loan that has slipped behind. Cash takes the repairs and showings out of the picture.

  1. Describe the house and give us the address.
  2. An offer comes back for the house exactly as it is.
  3. On acceptance, a title company or attorney handles the deed and the state return.
  4. Taxes, liens and payoffs come out of the proceeds.

Weigh the offer against a listing and against selling it yourself. The comparison that counts is what you take home after commission, repairs and the months it can take to get a buyer to closing.

Once you have an offer you like, a title company or attorney searches the title, confirms each payoff and prepares the deed and the conveyance tax return. The return is filed as the deed is recorded. Payoffs, including taxes and liens, are paid first, and the remainder goes to you.

Final utility readings happen in the same window, so tell the electric, water and heating suppliers the closing date once it is set. Your last bills then reflect your own use and nothing the buyer runs up.

If the Enfield Town Clerk files on paper, allow time for it. If a recorded lien turns up that you did not know about, tell the attorney right away, because it can usually be cleared with a payoff or a release but not overnight.

sections.h2: Matching the route to the house
sections.html:
A compact village house in Thompsonville and a rural parcel in the east are different properties with different buyers. Houses in the Presidential Section or in Scitico, with sidewalks and cul-de-sacs, usually appeal to buyers shopping for a suburban street, while a house in the historic district appeals to a narrower group who accept the age.

A house in good shape in one of the sought-after pockets may do best on the open market. If it is dated, vacant, tenant-occupied or inherited, a direct sale may fit better. We will tell you honestly which we think it is.

faqs.q: What are the main sections of Enfield?
faqs.a: Enfield Village, Thompsonville, Hazardville, Scitico and Sherwood Village.

faqs.q: Who do I call about Enfield property taxes?
faqs.a: Bills and due dates come from the Tax Collector, and your assessed value from the Assessor. The tax office can also supply a written payoff figure for closing.

faqs.q: Do I owe the Connecticut conveyance tax when I sell in Enfield?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes: a price of $2,000 or more is taxed unless an exemption fits, and the return goes in when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Can I sell an old Enfield house as it is?
faqs.a: Yes. Cash buyers take older houses in present condition and expect no repairs from you.

faqs.q: Does the historic district affect a sale in Enfield?
faqs.a: It can. Near the Enfield Historic District on Route 5, speak with town land use staff about exterior-work rules before you repair anything.
